Might or Mayhem? The State of the SANDF

By: Graham Coetzer | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In May 2021, President Cyril Ramaphosa announced sweeping changes to the millitary command of the SANDF - but many analysts say SA's millitary is on a downward spiral.

Unique Selling Point:
The July 2021 riots in KZN and Gauteng were a shocking reminder to many South Africans that the country's internal stability can never be taken for granted. Add to that the growing threat of insurgency in the north of Mozambique, instability in neighboring countries such as eSwatini and fears that another world war could break out amidst the ongoing Ukraine conflict, can the South African National Defence Force fulfill it's Constitutionally mandated task of defending South Africa and it's citizens?

Summary:
The new Minister of Defence, Thandi Modise, and new head of the SANDF General Rudzani Maphwanya have their work cut out for them if they are to achieve President Ramaphosa's envisioned "substantial change". A recent report to parliament's joint standing committee on defence highlighted some major issues facing the SANDF; for instance that of the 213 aircraft in the Airforce fleet, only 46 were serviceable. None of the 26 Gripen fighter jets owned by the SANDF are at this stage operational. Project Hoefyster, the SANDF's planned replacement of the outdated Ratel infantry vehicle, with 264 new combat vehicles called Badgers, is at a standstill, despite having R7 Billion spent on the project already, and it will cost another R16 Billion to complete it - another element of the ongoing implosion of DENEL. The navy is no better off, with 3 of our 4 frigates being cannibalised for spare parts to keep the last one afloat. Budgetary constraints are one of the major headaches for the SANDF, with the annual budget being cut yearly for the last few years. At the same time, Pres Ramaphosa has now greenlighted an extended deployment of the SANDF in Cabo del Gado (Operation Vikela) in Mozambique for another year, at a cost of R12.8 billion that was never budgeted for. Salaries are a huge expense, with many saying the SANDF is top heavy, and salaries make up 69% of the annual budget. (International average is 40%). This year the SANDF will exceed their budget on salaries to the tune of R2.7 billion. No wonder then that we struggle to even get soldiers deployed internally, such as during the July riots or the recent flooding in KZN.

Further information:
We have some great case studies, and have asked the Minister of Defence for an interview, as well as for an interview with General Maphwanya. If we don't get iether of those, we still have:

Helmoed Heitman - respected analyst, very fair and well informed, but not afraid to pull his punches.

Dr Moses Kanyile - Director of the Centre for Millitary Science - seems likely to tow the SANDF/Government line, which will be good for balance

Kobus Marais - shadow minister of defense and member of the defense oversight committee - has lots of insight into the state of affairs at DENEL /ARMSCOR, budget issues and equipment problems.

Prof Abel Esterhuyse - former LT Col in the SANDF and currently head of the dept of millitary strategy at the University of Stellenbosch - has great insight into the strategic issues, but brings the balance of having served in the SANDF for many years.

Godfrey Ramuhala - Currently completing his doctorate in millitary science at Stellenbosch, an outspoken but balanced analyst who is currently looking at many of the issues our story will cover.


Extra Budget Items:
Considering that many of the interviewees are in the Western Cape, it might be a good idea to spend one day down there. So:
Flights for presenter and producer, car rental for one day. No overnight accommodation needed.

Prof. Lindy Heinecken Military Socaiologist

Script:


State of the SANDF
First Draft Script
06 June 2022

Voice
In August 2013, South African soldiers deployed as peacekeepers in the Democratic Republic of Congo were involved in ongoing skirmishes with a hostile rebel group known as M23. They were part of a United Nations brigade mandated to meet force with force and drive the rebels from the notoriously volatile east of the country. During a fierce three-day battle, a South African Special Forces sniper shot and killed a rebel commander at an astonishing distance of 2125 metres – that’s more than 2km. At the time, it was the 6th longest confirmed sniper kill in history and another boost to the SANDF’s growing reputation in the DRC as a skilled combat force.
Just short of a decade later, that reputation is being eroded; not by complacency or a sudden drop off in skills, but because of a lack of money.  Simply put, the SANDF – heavily relied upon to keep civilians both here and elsewhere in Africa safe – is being strangled by a shrinking budget. And according to many, no longer fit for purpose.
Link Derek
For the Defence Force to fulfil their mandate of safeguarding the nation, they need the equipment to do so. But unfortunately the current reality is a rather sad state of affairs.

Voice
The force consists of roughly 73 000 personnel divided into four divisions: The South African Army, Navy, Airforce and Military Health Service. It’s their job to safeguard our borders, patrol our shores and assist with domestic threats. Respected defence analyst Helmoed Heitman says as government’s defence budget dwindled, maintenance lapsed on vital equipment such as our Swedish-made Gripen fighter jets.

Sound Up Helmoed Heitman
The entire Gripen fleet is grounded because they haven’t signed the support contract with SAAB.

Voice
Our fleet of Oryx helicopters meanwhile have suffered from the demise of state arms manufacturer, Denel.

Sound Up Helmoed Heitman
Of the Oryx fleet about half are not serviceable because of the problems at Denel and the Airforce hasn’t had money to pay Denel either.

Voice
In fact, the Defence Force’s acquisitions agency, Armscor, recently admitted that fewer than a quarter of the Airforce’s fleet was serviceable - meaning usable - with only 46 of 217 aircraft making the cut.

And the picture isn’t any rosier in the navy.

Sound Up Helmoed Heitman
Derek: Out of four frigates, you say only one is operational?

Helmoed: Well at the moment. Look a warship is a complex beast. More so than say a box boat. Of the four frigates, which are now roughly twenty plus years in service, only one has undergone a refit, and that’s only on the ship systems, not on the combat systems.

Voice
Our frigates have in the past been used to successfully curb piracy in the Mozambican channel and patrol our coastlines, but three of them are currently in dry dock.



Sound Up Helmoed
So they are still running on their twenty plus year old radars. Now sorry, military radars after 20 years are no longer what you might call cutting edge or anywhere near it.

Voice
But what about our 3 submarines, surely they’re operational?

Sound Up Helmoed
Of the submarines, only one has been refitted, and again only the ship systems.

Link Derek
It’s highly unlikely that we will face a conventional warfare threat to our country in the near future, but rampant crime, domestic instability and even natural disasters pose a significant threat to the state. So is it time to rethink the SANDF?

Voice
Defence Minister, Thandi Modise, believes it is. But maintaining a combat ready and nimble force takes money - and right now, she says our military is being thinly spread.

Sound Up Minister Modise
And I state this with a very heavy heart - we are willing but we lack resources. Unless there is a significant and quick intervention, our cupboards will remain bare.

Link Derek
So there’s the dilemma, the Defence Minister has been tasked with bringing about sweeping changes in the force, but even now she says she hasn’t got the budget to do it.

Voice
Enter General Rudzani Maphwanya, Defence Force Chief…

Sound Up General Rudzani Maphwanya
Your insurance for you to be able to say you will go to bed, and sleep, and have a dream of a better South Africa, and not a nightmare, that’s your Defence Force.

Voice
…appointed by president Cyril Ramaphosa last year and - like the minister - tasked with breathing life into into a Defence Force suffocating from a lack of funding.

Sound Up General Rudzani Maphwanya
The world over, the defence force is supposed to be at about 2% of the GDP. But our budget throughout the years had gone down such that we are currently operating with a budget that is below one percent of the GDP.

Voice
For comparison, Egypt - which has the largest military in Africa - spends around 2.4% of its Gross Domestic Product on defence, according to the world bank. So, says General Maphwanya, it’s time for a re-think.

Sound Up General Rudzani Maphwanya
Because what I had been doing previously, is it still relevant in today’s world?

Voice
Not according to Military Sociologist Professor Lindy Heinecken.

Sound Up Professor Lindy Heinecken
I would definitely look at training and preparing the Defence Force for more constabulary roles. These are roles that equip them with the ability to interact and protect citizens more effectively. Not as a primary goal for warfare.



Voice
In other words, a force more concerned with people’s welfare than with combat. It’s something the SANDF has already been doing, like curbing gang violence on the Cape Flats, or assisting in flood relief. Under a new plan to redesign the force, it may be something they do more - AND more efficiently.

Sound Up General Maphwanya
We have now, with the new Force Design, started positioning ourselves such that we should be able to respond quicker, to issues pertaining to any form of threat that is internal.

Voice
But, will this new design - a smaller, nimbler military - square with our government’s other ambitions? Will it continue to be pulled in several directions at the same time? President Ramaphosa has extended by another year the SANDF’s deployment in Mozambique where it’s helping fight insurgents in the Cabo del Gado region.

Sound Up Kobus Marais
Derek: Could we say that government is expecting too much from the Defence Force, for what it’s paying?

Kobus: Most certainly, most certainly. And the president is very keen on deploying the SANDF. You know the 1000 now to the DRC, the 1495 now to the Cabo Del Gado in Mozambique.

Voice
Kobus Marais, is the DA’s shadow minister for Defence, and says the Mozambique mission will cost an extra R2.8 billion - money that wasn’t budgeted for.

Sound Up Kobus
If you authorise deployment that was over and above the budget process, you have to provide additional funding. Otherwise it is stealing from Peter to pay Paul, and that is just exacerbating the spiralling down of the capabilities of the Defence Force.

Voice
And yet there’s at least good reason to maintain the foreign deployments, tight as money is: despite what many believe about the Defence Force - on performance standards alone - it remains a respected fighting force. In the DRC for example, it enjoys a fierce reputation.

Sound Up Helmoed Heitman
Two different Monusco commanders have said the only battalion they’d be prepared to go to war with, is a South African one. They’ve said that over a couple of years now.

Voice
That’s good news for the DRC, but what about threats closer to home?

Sound Up Helmoed Heitman
Derek: If a hostile aircraft entered South African airspace, how could we respond?

Helmoed: Well if the Gripens were operational we can, but while they aren’t we can’t. The other thing is our radar coverage is a bit limited. But at this stage, if you detect it coming in, say right there is an unidentified aircraft coming in, the airforce will say well sorry, oops.

Voice
But hope is on the horizon.

Sound Up General Maphwanya
I want to tell you something that will make you go to bed and sleep at least at ease…





Voice
As he and his team hammer out a new budget and structure for the defence force, General Maphwanya says a deal has been struck with SAAB, the manufacturers of the Gripen fighter jets, that’ll get them back in the air and keep them there.

And they’re working on getting more choppers off the ground, too.

Sound Up General Maphwanya
We have moved out of the box in terms of acquiring spares for our Oryx and Rooivalk.

Voice
In times of peace it’s often difficult to justify spending money much needed elsewhere on the defence of the country, and it remains to be seen whether the new hands on deck will eventually convince cabinet to increase their budget.

Sound Up Prof Heinecken
Some hard decisions will have to be taken, as to what is our priorities. It’s like an insurance policy. You need to decide, you know, what insurance are you going to let go, and what is the most important that you need to maintain.

Voice
The way forward will be a difficult balancing act. While the Defence Force is fighting for its life, its expertise are becoming increasingly important in an ever changing world.

Sound Up Helmoed Heitman
Despite everything, the underfunding, and let’s be honest, there have been some senior appointments that are very strange, that can only be explained politically. And that were done over the heads of the chief and the minister in some cases, and that I happen to know. But depsite that, every time a new job gets tossed at the defence force they somehow come to the party, grab it out of the hat, and do the job. And usually they do it quite well.

Voice
A sentiment shared by the General.




























Promo 1 (21 Sec)

Sound Up Explosion

Voice
The South African National Defence Force still enjoys an enviable reputation across Africa. But it’s also being eroded; not by complacency or a sudden drop off in skills, but because of a lack of money.(11)

Sound Up Helmoed
The entire Gripen fleet is grounded because they haven’t signed the support contract with SAAB. (4)

Voice
Can it be saved and is it time to rethink the SANDF? (9)



Promo 2

Voice
There’s a new boss in town at the Defence Force, and he says he’s ready to drag it kicking and screaming into the 21st century (8)

Sound Up General Maphwanya
and have a dream of a better South Africa, and not a nightmare, that’s your Defence Force

Voice
A closer look at the SANDF. (4)


Promo 3
There’s a new chief in town - can General Rudzani Maphwanya resuscitate the Defence Force, especially in a world facing ever changing threats?

Sound Up General Maphwanya We have now, with the new Force Design, started positioning ourselves such that we should be able to respond quicker, to issues pertaining to any form of threat that is internal. Voice But, will this new design - a smaller, nimbler military - square with our government’s other ambitions? Will it continue to be pulled in several directions at the same time? President Ramaphosa has extended by another year the SANDF’s deployment in Mozambique where it’s helping fight insurgents in the Cabo del Gado region. Sound Up Kobus Marais Derek: Could we say that government is expecting too much from the Defence Force, for what it’s paying? Kobus: Most certainly, most certainly. And the president is very keen on deploying the SANDF. You know the 1000 now to the DRC, the 1495 now to the Cabo Del Gado in Mozambique. Voice Kobus Marais, is the DA’s shadow minister for Defence, and says the Mozambique mission will cost an extra R2.8 billion - money that wasn’t budgeted for. Sound Up Kobus If you authorise deployment that was over and above the budget process, you have to provide additional funding. Otherwise it is stealing from Peter to pay Paul, and that is just exacerbating the spiralling down of the capabilities of the Defence Force. Voice And yet there’s at least good reason to maintain the foreign deployments, tight as money is: despite what many believe about the Defence Force - on performance standards alone - it remains a respected fighting force. In the DRC for example, it enjoys a fierce reputation. Sound Up Helmoed Heitman Two different Monusco commanders have said the only battalion they’d be prepared to go to war with, is a South African one. They’ve said that over a couple of years now. Voice That’s good news for the DRC, but what about threats closer to home? Sound Up Helmoed Heitman Derek: If a hostile aircraft entered South African airspace, how could we respond? Helmoed: Well if the Gripens were operational we can, but while they aren’t we can’t. The other thing is our radar coverage is a bit limited. But at this stage, if you detect it coming in, say right there is an unidentified aircraft coming in, the airforce will say well sorry, oops. Voice But hope is on the horizon. Sound Up General Maphwanya I want to tell you something that will make you go to bed and sleep at least at ease… Voice As he and his team hammer out a new budget and structure for the defence force, General Maphwanya says a deal has been struck with SAAB, the manufacturers of the Gripen fighter jets, that’ll get them back in the air and keep them there. And they’re working on getting more choppers off the ground, too. Sound Up General Maphwanya We have moved out of the box in terms of acquiring spares for our Oryx and Rooivalk. Voice In times of peace it’s often difficult to justify spending money much needed elsewhere on the defence of the country, and it remains to be seen whether the new hands on deck will eventually convince cabinet to increase their budget. Sound Up Prof Heinecken Some hard decisions will have to be taken, as to what is our priorities. It’s like an insurance policy. You need to decide, you know, what insurance are you going to let go, and what is the most important that you need to maintain. Voice The way forward will be a difficult balancing act. While the Defence Force is fighting for its life, its expertise are becoming increasingly important in an ever changing world. Sound Up Helmoed Heitman Despite everything, the underfunding, and let’s be honest, there have been some senior appointments that are very strange, that can only be explained politically. And that were done over the heads of the chief and the minister in some cases, and that I happen to know. But depsite that, every time a new job gets tossed at the defence force they somehow come to the party, grab it out of the hat, and do the job. And usually they do it quite well. Voice A sentiment shared by the General. Promo 1 (21 Sec) Sound Up Explosion Voice The South African National Defence Force still enjoys an enviable reputation across Africa. But it’s also being eroded; not by complacency or a sudden drop off in skills, but because of a lack of money.(11) Sound Up Helmoed The entire Gripen fleet is grounded because they haven’t signed the support contract with SAAB. (4) Voice Can it be saved and is it time to rethink the SANDF? (9) Promo 2 Voice There’s a new boss in town at the Defence Force, and he says he’s ready to drag it kicking and screaming into the 21st century (8) Sound Up General Maphwanya and have a dream of a better South Africa, and not a nightmare, that’s your Defence Force Voice A closer look at the SANDF. (4) Promo 3 There’s a new chief in town - can General Rudzani Maphwanya resuscitate the Defence Force, especially in a world facing ever changing threats?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In May 2021, President Cyril Ramaphosa announced sweeping changes to the millitary command of the SANDF - but many analysts say SA's millitary is on a downward spiral.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The July 2021 riots in KZN and Gauteng were a shocking reminder to many South Africans that the country's internal stability can never be taken for granted. Add to that the growing threat of insurgency in the north of Mozambique, instability in neighboring countries such as eSwatini and fears that another world war could break out amidst the ongoing Ukraine conflict, can the South African National Defence Force fulfill it's Constitutionally mandated task of defending South Africa and it's citizens?
metadata.Summary: The new Minister of Defence, Thandi Modise, and new head of the SANDF General Rudzani Maphwanya have their work cut out for them if they are to achieve President Ramaphosa's envisioned "substantial change". A recent report to parliament's joint standing committee on defence highlighted some major issues facing the SANDF; for instance that of the 213 aircraft in the Airforce fleet, only 46 were serviceable. None of the 26 Gripen fighter jets owned by the SANDF are at this stage operational. Project Hoefyster, the SANDF's planned replacement of the outdated Ratel infantry vehicle, with 264 new combat vehicles called Badgers, is at a standstill, despite having R7 Billion spent on the project already, and it will cost another R16 Billion to complete it - another element of the ongoing implosion of DENEL. The navy is no better off, with 3 of our 4 frigates being cannibalised for spare parts to keep the last one afloat. Budgetary constraints are one of the major headaches for the SANDF, with the annual budget being cut yearly for the last few years. At the same time, Pres Ramaphosa has now greenlighted an extended deployment of the SANDF in Cabo del Gado (Operation Vikela) in Mozambique for another year, at a cost of R12.8 billion that was never budgeted for. Salaries are a huge expense, with many saying the SANDF is top heavy, and salaries make up 69% of the annual budget. (International average is 40%). This year the SANDF will exceed their budget on salaries to the tune of R2.7 billion. No wonder then that we struggle to even get soldiers deployed internally, such as during the July riots or the recent flooding in KZN.
metadata.Further information: We have some great case studies, and have asked the Minister of Defence for an interview, as well as for an interview with General Maphwanya. If we don't get iether of those, we still have: Helmoed Heitman - respected analyst, very fair and well informed, but not afraid to pull his punches. Dr Moses Kanyile - Director of the Centre for Millitary Science - seems likely to tow the SANDF/Government line, which will be good for balance Kobus Marais - shadow minister of defense and member of the defense oversight committee - has lots of insight into the state of affairs at DENEL /ARMSCOR, budget issues and equipment problems. Prof Abel Esterhuyse - former LT Col in the SANDF and currently head of the dept of millitary strategy at the University of Stellenbosch - has great insight into the strategic issues, but brings the balance of having served in the SANDF for many years. Godfrey Ramuhala - Currently completing his doctorate in millitary science at Stellenbosch, an outspoken but balanced analyst who is currently looking at many of the issues our story will cover.
